title: Federal policy changes are putting Maryland’s businesses under severe strain
summary: Rising costs, taxes and tariffs, and an uncertain future for federal jobs and contracts have combined to put a strain on Maryland businesses, writes Kislaya Prasad, but at least some in his recent poll remain optimistic for the coming year.
content:
by Kislaya Prasad, Maryland Matters January 7, 2026

by Kislaya Prasad, Maryland Matters January 7, 2026

It has been a difficult year for Maryland businesses. This is especially true for the many businesses that do business with the federal government. They have faced disruptions caused by federal reductions in force (RIFs) as well as sweeping changes in federal contracting and procurement policies. Companies have also been affected by an increase in tariff rates. And some state taxes have increased as well.

I and my colleagues have just completed a detailed survey to assess where Maryland businesses stand as we head toward the end of 2025. The survey asked respondents about this past year’s performance relative to 2024, their outlook over the next six months, the impact of federal policy changes, and their views of Maryland as a place to do business. Respondents also provided open-ended comments, and these attest to the very human costs behind the topline findings.

Overall, the survey paints a picture of a business community under pressure from rising costs and shifting federal and trade policies. Performance in 2025 was weaker than in 2024 for about half the firms in our sample of more than 90 companies. Still, many are cautiously optimistic about the next six months.

Rising costs remain a major challenge: roughly 80% of respondents reported higher costs, and most expect the trend to continue. These cost pressures have translated into higher prices. When asked to identify the most significant challenge of 2025, respondents highlighted rising costs, federal policy disruptions, and weak sales. As one put it, “The Maryland economy now faces unprecedented challenges and struggle, compounded by electricity price surges and costs.”

Federal policy changes have been especially disruptive. Many firms – particularly those heavily involved in federal contracting – reported negative impacts from RIFs and from changes in procurement and contracting policies. Staffing cuts have delayed payments and created administrative bottlenecks. One firm noted: “Contract officers are untrained, payments for services rendered are delayed, putting financial strain on small businesses.”

In some cases, contracts, grants and anticipated solicitations have been canceled altogether: “Federal contracting has almost completely dried up for us. Option years have been canceled or significantly de-scoped for most of our multi-year contracts.” However, a small number of respondents did report positive outcomes, most often in the aerospace and defense sector.

Other policy-related impacts also surfaced in the comments. The termination of programs supporting minority and economically disadvantaged businesses, as well as environmental initiatives, was noted repeatedly. One firm wrote: “We feel as if we are now working against our own federal government, which is trying to kill the solar industry.” Another pointed to the erosion of protections for socially/economically disadvantaged and minority-owned businesses. Respondents also highlighted a trend toward contract bundling – the practice of combining multiple contracts into fewer, larger awards – which tends to favor large firms over small.

Trade policy has introduced its own set of pressures for firms. Many companies reported that new tariffs have raised the cost of imported inputs and reduced supply chain reliability, although a few cited benefits from reduced foreign competition. Firms reported shifting sourcing countries, moving from international to domestic suppliers, and stockpiling critical inputs to manage disruptions.

Finally, we asked about Maryland’s business environment. Many firms view it unfavorably, and some reported having considered relocating to another state. High taxes, high operating costs, and housing affordability were top concerns. One respondent captured the sentiment bluntly: “Maryland is not a business-friendly state. We are at the point we can no longer afford the taxes that continue to go up and up.”

The recent increase in the sales and use tax on data and IT services was cited by several firms: “The 3% Technology Tax makes it difficult to compete with firms in VA, DE, and PA that do not have such a burden.” If there is a silver lining, it is that minority-owned businesses were somewhat less likely to view Maryland as unhospitable.

The survey does not suggest a uniformly dire situation, and many firms remain optimistic about the months ahead. Maryland’s talent base and proximity to federal agencies continue to be viewed as advantages. However, it is hard to escape the conclusion that the state has pressing structural issues that require urgent attention. Maryland businesses also need to adapt to a new reality of changed federal policies and priorities. Our finding that policy disruptions are hitting some firms much harder than others points to how support can be appropriately targeted while firms adjust to the new reality.
